tagline: Across the Ozarks, old highway alignments lead toward the Mississippi.
intro: Historic Route 66 crosses Missouri from the Kansas line west of Joplin toward St. Louis and the Mississippi. The drive includes Ozark terrain, a grape-growing district between St. James and Sullivan, and steep bluffs beside the older highway through Pacific. FHWA includes Missouri in its Historic Route 66 entry under National Scenic Byway and All-American Road designations. The Route 66 Association of Missouri promotes the corridor through its history and culture.

Between St. Louis and Springfield, an earlier route was known as the Osage Indian Trail. A telegraph line laid along the road by the mid-nineteenth century gave it the name Wire Road; after the line came down, it became Old Wire Road. The numbered highway followed in 1926, then underwent repeated realignments. I-44 later took over much of its traffic corridor. The marked historic alignment in Missouri uses the 1935 route as its basis, preserving one stage in that changing road.

Heading east, trace the old road through Joplin and Carthage toward Springfield. Continue through Lebanon and Waynesville to Devils Elbow, then Rolla and the country near Meramec Caverns at Stanton. Near St. Louis, successive alignments used different river crossings. Chain of Rocks carried Bypass US 66; that historic bridge now serves walking and cycling trails.
notice: At Pacific, the older highway passes beneath steep bluffs.

moments.title: Devils Elbow
moments.text: The Big Piney’s sharp bend made trouble for the rafters who floated lumber and railroad ties downstream. Rafts broke apart and ties were lost, giving the bend its name: Devil’s Elbow. Road builders crossed the river with a steel truss bridge in 1923 as part of improvements to State Highway 14. That highway became US 66 in 1926. A divided four-lane alignment bypassed the community in late 1945, reducing highway traffic. The original alignment through the hamlet is now called Teardrop Road. The later alignment on Highway Z bypasses the hamlet, crossing the river beyond a cut through a steep hillside.

moments.title: Meramec Caverns
moments.text: Meramec Caverns hosted square dances before Lester B. Dill introduced the extended cave system as a tourist attraction in 1935. The Ballroom was first used in 1890 for square dances and other community events. The cavern system near Stanton extends 4.6 miles. Its uses reach beyond tourism: saltpeter was extracted here during the eighteenth century to make gunpowder. In 1972, the caverns supplied settings for the musical film Tom Sawyer, released the following year. Inside, grape-like mineral clusters decorate the Wine Room and its Wine Table, a formation supported by three natural legs.

moments.title: Chain of Rocks Bridge
moments.text: Chain of Rocks Bridge turns 22 degrees in the middle of its Mississippi crossing. During construction, a water intake and bedrock unable to bear the bridge’s weight made the bend necessary. Built privately as a toll bridge in 1929, it became part of Bypass US 66 in the late 1930s. The bypass took traffic past the northern and western sides of St. Louis, avoiding downtown. The old bridge closed in 1970; in 1998, Trailnet leased it for a new role serving walkers and cyclists. The bridge links the Missouri shore to Chouteau Island on the Illinois side of the river.
moments.notice: The bridge’s 22-degree bend interrupts the line of the crossing.

practical: Chain of Rocks Bridge: The old Chain of Rocks Bridge carries walking and cycling trails only; vehicle traffic uses the New Chain of Rocks Bridge to the north. (checked 2026-10-11)
